name: Santa Catarina
summary:
Santa Catarina is the only Brazilian state to have enacted a statutory bathroom restriction binding a visitor: Lei nº 19.686 of 21 January 2026 (signed by Governor Jorginho Mello 26 Jan 2026) mandates sex-separated facilities in all educational institutions with fines up to R$10,000, and PL 491/2021 (approved 22 Dec 2025) extends the ban to state and municipal public-administration buildings. A further escalation bill (PL 771/2025) would restrict locker rooms to birth-certificate sex. These are enacted, enforceable rules, not aspirational statutes.

The decisive national precedent came from this state: on 6 June 2024 the STF rejected the appeal of a trans woman refused the women's bathroom at a Florianópolis shopping centre, leaving the refusal lawful under private-premises rules (RE 845.779/SC). ANTRA, ABGLT and IBRAT subsequently denounced Brazil to the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights (Aug 2025), confirming the incident crossed an international threshold.

These legal findings put SC well below the national 0.71: a visitor presenting visibly in a school, public office, or shopping centre faces actual exclusion backed by statute and a favourable high-court precedent. By contrast, Paraná (0.71) has no enacted facility rule and no comparable judicial finding. The STF's national criminalisation of LGBT+ phobia (2019) still applies, and SC's violence numbers are not among the worst, so the penalty is not as steep as the killing hotspots—but the legal exposure is uniquely concrete.

name: Ceara
summary:
Ceará is the most consistent lethal hotspot for trans and travesti people in the Northeast: 11 killings in 2024 (3rd nationally, 1st in the region) and 8 in 2025 (tied for the highest state total in the country). Against a population of ~9 million this yields roughly 0.9 killings per million per year—more than double the national rate of ~0.38/million (80 / 213 M). The 2025 dossier further notes a concentration of Black victims in Ceará.

This places Ceará about 0.10 below the national 0.71. The deviation is driven by sustained, patterned lethal exposure rather than any legal distinction (the federal constitution and penal code apply uniformly). Compared with Minas Gerais (0.64), which matched Ceará's absolute 2025 count of 8, Minas Gerais' much larger population (~21 M) gives a per-capita rate at the national average, making Ceará the higher-risk state on a rate basis.

For a visibly trans visitor, the pattern matters: the killings are concentrated on young Black trans women in public space—precisely the exposure profile of a conspicuous traveller—and the consistency across two years signals an entrenched environment rather than a statistical blip.

name: Rio Granda do Norte
summary:
Rio Grande do Norte recorded zero trans killings in 2024 but jumped to 4 in 2025—the sharpest deterioration in the ANTRA dataset. Against a population of ~3.5 million, four cases yields approximately 1.14 killings per million per year, the highest per-capita rate among all 27 units in 2025 and roughly three times the national figure of ~0.38/million. The dossier cautions against reading a single-year zero as safety and notes the volatility.

This rate-driven exposure puts RN about 0.11 below the national 0.71. Compared with Ceará (0.61), RN's absolute count is lower (4 vs 8) but the per-capita risk is actually higher; the deviation from national is therefore slightly larger than one might expect from the raw numbers. The state sits within the Northeast bloc that accounted for 38 of 80 national killings in 2025.

No state-level statutory restriction or unique legal finding applies; the risk is purely a violence-rate signal. For a visitor, the small absolute numbers mean a single incident dramatically shifts perception, and the volatility suggests the environment can turn rapidly.

name: Paraiba
summary:
Paraíba recorded 4 killings of trans and travesti people in 2025, the same absolute count as Rio Grande do Norte. Against a population of ~4 million this yields approximately 1.0 per million per year—well above the national rate of ~0.38/million and among the highest in the federation. The state is part of the Northeast bloc that absorbed 38 of 80 national killings (47.5%) in 2025.

The per-capita rate places Paraíba roughly 0.09 below the national 0.71. Compared with Alagoas (0.68), which had 2 killings in a similar population (~3.3 M, rate ~0.61/million), Paraíba's absolute count is double and its rate higher, reflecting the broader Northeast concentration on a smaller denominator.

No Paraíba-specific legal or ordinance evidence was found; the deviation is driven entirely by the violence dataset. The victim profile—young, Black, poor, Northeastern—concentrates risk on individuals who present visibly in public space.

name: Minas Gerais
summary:
Minas Gerais ranked 2nd nationally in 2024 with 12 killings and tied for the top in 2025 with 8 (matching Ceará). Against a population of ~21 million, the 2025 rate of ~0.38/million sits at the national average, but the consistency of appearing in the top two every year signals a structurally elevated environment compared with states that fluctuate. The 2024 total of 12 placed it behind only São Paulo.

These factors put Minas Gerais about 0.07 below the national 0.71. Compared with Ceará (0.61), which matched the same 2025 absolute count on a much smaller population, Minas Gerais' per-capita exposure is roughly half—so the deviation is more moderate. Compared with São Paulo (no deviation recorded), which led the 2024 count at 16 but fell sharply in 2025, Minas Gerais' consistency across both years is the distinguishing risk factor.

No state-specific legal restriction or unique ordinance was identified. The risk for a visitor is violence-exposure, patterned over two years, in a large interior state where the 68%-outside-capitals finding of the 2024 dossier implies elevated risk away from Belo Horizonte.

name: Pernambuco
summary:
Pernambuco recorded 7 killings of trans and travesti people in 2025, placing it in the second tier behind Ceará/Minas Gerais. Against a population of ~9.4 million this yields roughly 0.74 per million per year—nearly double the national rate. Crucially, the state hosts the major tourist corridor of Recife and Olinda, so the violence concentration directly overlaps with visitor traffic and visible trans presence in public coastal spaces.

The rate and tourism overlap put Pernambuco about 0.07 below the national 0.71. Compared with Bahia (0.65), which also recorded 7 killings in 2025, Bahia's larger population (~15 M) gives a lower per-capita rate of ~0.47/million; Pernambuco's risk density is therefore somewhat higher despite the identical absolute count, and both states share the visitor-coast exposure.

No Pernambuco-specific legal restriction or ordinance was found. The deviation is violence-driven and location-dependent: a trans visitor staying in Recife's centre or the Olida historic district is in the same geography where the killings cluster.

name: Bahia
summary:
Bahia recorded 7 killings of trans and travesti people in 2025, the same absolute count as Pernambuco and the second tier nationally. Against a population of ~15 million the rate is approximately 0.47 per million per year, above the national 0.38/million but below Ceará and Pernambuco. Bahia's coast—Salvador, the beaches—draws substantial tourist traffic, and the violence data overlaps with visitor areas.

These findings place Bahia about 0.06 below the national 0.71. Compared with Pernambuco (0.64), which matched the absolute count on a smaller population (higher rate), Bahia's per-capita exposure is somewhat lower, justifying the small positive delta. Compared with the national average, Bahia is a mid-high risk state driven by Northeast-region concentration (38 of 80 killings in 2025) rather than by any local legal distinction.

No Bahia-specific ordinance or statutory restriction was identified. The risk is a violence gradient within the broader Northeast pattern, with tourism overlap raising visitor exposure above what the per-capita rate alone suggests.

name: Rio de Jeneiro
summary:
Rio de Janeiro recorded only 3 trans killings in 2025 (a low rate of ~0.18/million against a population of ~17 M), well below the national average. However, two distinct visitor-facing signals pull the score modestly below the national 0.71: a documented extortion pattern in Niterói and a tourist-targeting scam in Copacabana.

In January–February 2026, multiple trans sex workers in central Niterói reported a two-year coercive regime: a man claiming militia and public-agent connections forced them to pay R$120 per week each and had 'almost strangled three of the girls.' The alleged extorter was an ex-employee of Niterói city hall, arrested in 'Operação Ronda Sumbria' by the 76ª DP, and remanded in pre-trial custody. The institutional response was mixed—arrests and dismissal occurred, but the racket operated under the appearance of state backing for roughly two years before intervention. Trans council member Benny Briolly brought the case to the Public Ministry.

Separately, in Copacabana the tourist police (Deat) arrested two trans women caught extorting a Norwegian tourist with threats to circulate intimate videos—a documented, visitor-facing scam vector. The killing rate is low, but the coercive pattern with state implication and the tourist-targeting scam justify a deviation of about 0.03 below national. Compared with São Paulo (no deviation), Rio's risk is qualitative rather than numerical.

name: Goias
summary:
Goiás recorded 5 killings of trans and travesti people in 2025, placing it in the mid-band alongside Maranhão and Pará. Against a population of ~7.2 million the rate is approximately 0.69 per million per year, about 1.8× the national rate of 0.38/million. Goiás sits on the Cerrado agricultural frontier, and the dossier notes that 68% of 2024 killings occurred outside state capitals—in interior towns where a visitor's exposure may be harder to mitigate.

The rate and absence of any mitigating legal or institutional finding place Goiás about 0.04 below the national 0.71. Compared with Minas Gerais (0.64), which had 8 killings in 2025, Goiás' lower absolute count partly reflects a smaller population, but the per-capita gap (0.69 vs 0.38/million) is directionally consistent with a moderate deviation. No Goiás-specific ordinance or statutory restriction was identified.

name: Maranhao
summary:
Maranhão recorded 5 killings of trans and travesti people in 2025, the same absolute count as Goiás and Pará. Against a population of ~7.1 million the rate is approximately 0.70 per million per year, nearly double the national average. Maranhão is one of the poorest states in the federation, and the dossier's victim profile—young, Black, poor, Northeastern—maps directly onto the state's demographics, suggesting the killings are not incidental but patterned along the structural inequalities that make trans visibility most dangerous.

The rate and poverty-driven vulnerability place Maranhão about 0.04 below the national 0.71. Compared with Ceará (0.61), which shares the Northeast concentration but recorded 8 killings on a smaller population (rate ~0.89/million), Maranhão's risk is somewhat lower but in the same directional band. No unit-specific legal or ordinance evidence was found.

name: Para
summary:
Pará recorded 5 killings of trans and travesti people in 2025, matching the Goiás/Maranhão band. Against a population of ~8.7 million the rate is approximately 0.57 per million per year, above the national 0.38/million. Pará spans the Amazon region, where the 68%-outside-capitals finding means interior municipal exposure is difficult to assess and infrastructure for protection is thinner.

The above-national rate and geographic risk-concentration place Pará about 0.04 below the national 0.71. Compared with Ceará (0.61), which had 8 killings on ~9 million (rate ~0.89/million), Pará is less severe on a per-capita basis, but the Amazonian interior geography amplifies the difficulty of accessing help after an incident for a visitor. No Pará-specific legal or ordinance finding was identified.

name: Alagoas
summary:
Alagoas recorded 2 killings of trans and travesti people in 2025. Against a population of ~3.3 million the rate is approximately 0.61 per million per year, above the national average but below the Ceará/Paraíba/Rio Grande do Norte cluster. Alagoas is part of the Northeast bloc that absorbed 38 of 80 national killings in 2025, so the unit sits in a region of elevated violence even though its own absolute count is modest.

The above-national rate and regional concentration justify a deviation of about 0.03 below the national 0.71. Compared with Paraíba (0.62), which recorded 4 killings on a similar population (rate ~1.0/million), Alagoas is materially less severe, and the small absolute number (2) means a single case would shift the rate dramatically. No unit-specific legal restriction or enforcement finding was identified.

name: Mato Grosso
summary:
Mato Grosso recorded 3 killings of trans and travesti people in 2025. Against a population of ~3.6 million the rate is approximately 0.83 per million per year—more than double the national rate of 0.38/million. The state sits on the Cerrado/agribusiness frontier, an area where the 68%-outside-capitals pattern means small-town exposure is relevant for a visitor travelling beyond Cuiabá.

The elevated per-capita rate places Mato Grosso about 0.02 below the national 0.71, the minimum threshold for a record. The deviation is modest because 3 cases on a small population is statistically fragile and no qualitative incident, ordinance, or enforcement evidence was found beyond the ANTRA count. Compared with Goiás (0.67), which recorded 5 killings on ~7.2 million (rate ~0.69/million), Mato Grosso's per-capita figure is actually higher, but the smaller absolute count and absence of corroborating detail justify a smaller deviation.

name: Distrito Federal
summary:
The Distrito Federal recorded 2 killings of trans and travesti people in 2025, a low absolute count for a major metropolitan area. Brasília is the seat of the STF, the national protective apparatus, and the offices of human-rights bodies; ANTRA's own Dossiê is compiled and reported from DF desks. The capital hosts international diplomatic missions and NGO infrastructure that raise the visibility and institutional cost of anti-trans violence.

These factors justify a modest positive deviation of about 0.02 above the national 0.71. Compared with São Paulo (0.71, no deviation), which also leads in institutional capacity but recorded 4 killings in 2025 and 16 in 2024, the DF's lower absolute numbers and concentration of protective infrastructure make it marginally safer for a visitor. The 2 killings against ~3 million population give a rate of ~0.67/million—above the national average in per-capita terms—so the positive deviation is qualitative (institutional visibility, international presence) rather than purely numerical.
